title: J3 — Made official
description: A nurse verifies the cards are genuine and fits the Thai doses into the Lao schedule.

steps.title: The clinic confirms the cards are genuine
steps.headline: Nurse Chanthasone scans the card, and her tablet checks Thailand’s digital signature against the WHO trust list — without contacting Thailand.

preconditions.title: The DID documents are already loaded
preconditions.description: **Precondition: the DID documents are already loaded.** Loading them is not a step of this visit. The clinic may be offline all day, so the EHR fetches nothing during it: its trust store holds the GDHCN DEV trust list as it was last refreshed, including XXR's DSC DID document (STT-TRU-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-TRU-005). A clinic with no connection of its own refreshes it about weekly, when the CHW visits the base clinic or district health office, where Country B retrieves the list the GDHCN trust anchor distributes. A DSC published after that refresh is not in the clinic's copy, so its DVC fails the trust-list check (STT-VER-006) until the next refresh.

steps.narrative:
Nurse Chanthasone opens the referral and scans the QRs. The EHR
**verifies** each DVC offline against that copy (STT-VER-001…009,
STT-KID-002), without contacting Thailand. Both verify, so it imports them as
FHIR `Immunization`s (`TrustDemoJ3HepB`, `TrustDemoJ3Bcg`) with provenance
(`TrustDemoJ3Verification`; STT-VER-007, STT-VER-008), replacing the reported
doses of J2. If a DVC fails (a tampered card, say), the EHR names the step and
the reason, the doses stay unverified, and the nurse decides by national
catch-up policy.

experiences.doing: Scans the card; the tablet confirms the Thai signature and marks the doses verified.
experiences.feeling: “A green tick — I can trust a hospital I’ve never heard of.”

experiences.doing: Brings Somsack in for the referral visit.

steps.painPoint: Clinicians either distrust foreign paper and re-vaccinate, or trust it blindly.
steps.enabler: Thailand’s signing key is on the shared WHO trust list, so any clinic can check it locally.
steps.policy: Trust is decentralized: a Lao clinic verifies a Thai signature itself, without contacting Thailand.

record.description: Doses verified; Thailand recorded as the source

whatIf.scenario: The card has been tampered with.
whatIf.outcome: The signature check fails, the doses stay unverified and the nurse follows the local catch-up policy.

steps.technicalSummary: The clinic checks Thailand’s signature against WHO’s trust list, stored locally. One check turns a foreign paper card into trusted clinical data, with no call to Thailand.

uses.role: Clinic tablet app; caches the trust list
Delivers the CHW’s referral to this clinic; the nurse can only see patients referred to her facility
Supplies Thailand’s public key (downloaded in advance)
Records that Thailand authored and Lao PDR verified the doses

illustration.alt: At the district health centre, Nurse Chanthasone checks the cards on a tablet: signature verified, on the Lao schedule; Khamla and Bounmy hold Somsack

fhirChanges.why: A verified DVC is the signing hospital’s own record, so the dose now counts; the Thai record it came from is unchanged.

fhirChanges.change: Created: author = Thailand MOPH, verifier = nurse
fhirChanges.why: Anyone who later doubts a dose can follow it back to the signed certificate and Thailand’s key.

steps.title: Thai vaccines are fitted to the Lao schedule
steps.headline: The Thai Hep B product doesn’t match anything on the Lao schedule. Chanthasone makes the clinical call, and the system works out what’s due next.
steps.narrative:
The Thai Hep B product matches nothing on the national schedule.
The EHR keeps Thailand's product coding and adds the schedule coding beside
it, from the national map (`TrustDemoProductToLaoEpi`). For the Hep B product
the map has no entry, so Nurse Chanthasone makes the clinical call that it is
the schedule's birth dose (`TrustDemoJ3Adjudication`), and her decision is
added to the map for the next clinic. The schedule (`TrustDemoLaoInfantSchedule`)
then runs: the birth doses count, and pentavalent 1, bOPV 1 and PCV 1 are due
at 6 weeks (`TrustDemoJ3Recommendation`). Khamla leaves with the date
(`TrustDemoJ3Reminder`). Over the year Somsack gets those doses and
measles-rubella at 9 months, in Lao PDR.

experiences.doing: Confirms the Thai product equals the Lao birth dose; the system books the 6-week vaccines.
experiences.feeling: “Different name, same vaccine — I can make that call.”

experiences.doing: Leaves with a date for Somsack’s next vaccines.
experiences.feeling: “Now I know exactly when to come back.”

steps.painPoint: Countries name and package vaccines differently, so doses get missed or repeated.
steps.enabler: Thailand’s original code is kept and the Lao code is added alongside; the schedule engine calculates what’s due.
steps.policy: Never overwrite another country’s record: keep the original coding alongside the national one.

record.description: Birth doses count; next appointment booked

handoff.summary: Somsack continues on the Lao schedule for a year

whatIf.scenario: There is no automatic match for the foreign vaccine.
whatIf.outcome: That is exactly this step. The nurse decides — and her decision could be shared so the next nurse doesn’t have to.

steps.technicalSummary: Shared WHO codes and a FHIR ConceptMap translate Thai vaccines into the Lao schedule. Computable schedule logic then works out what’s due next.

uses.role: Common PreQual codes make the mapping possible
PreQual product → WHO vaccine type → Lao EPI code
Lao schedule logic calculates the 6-week doses
Saves dual-coded record and syncs it to the national server
Checks the nurse’s role and facility before accepting the update
Verified Thai doses, with their Provenance, count toward Lao coverage reports

illustration.alt: At the district health centre, Nurse Chanthasone checks the cards on a tablet: signature verified, on the Lao schedule; Khamla and Bounmy hold Somsack

fhirChanges.change: Lao EPI code added; PreQual code kept
fhirChanges.why: The Lao schedule runs on Lao EPI codes, so one is required; the Thai product code stays beside it, never overwritten.
Lao PDR’s own map from vaccine products to its schedule; a product with no mapping goes to the nurse.
The Lao schedule (PlanDefinition) finds the 6-week doses due; the reminder brings him back.
